analysis.summary: The PR introduces Salesforce-specific logic paths that are inconsistent with existing service signatures and standard data structures, likely leading to runtime failures and undefined parameters.

bugs.title: Incomplete Function Signature Update for getUserOrder
bugs.description: While 'cancelOrder' was updated in core to accept 'Partial<EcomAuthenticatedHeaders>', 'getUserOrder' was not. The Salesforce path in 'get-orders' now passes a partial header object (containing only 'user-id' and 'base-site-id') to 'getUserOrder'.
bugs.risk: If 'getUserOrder' still expects full 'EcomAuthenticatedHeaders' (e.g., requiring 'authorization' or other tokens), the service will fail at runtime or cause downstream authentication errors.

bugs.title: Header Property Name Mismatch (Kebab-case vs Camel-case)
bugs.description: The Salesforce logic paths manually construct header objects using raw kebab-case keys (e.g., 'base-site-id') instead of the camel-case properties (e.g., 'baseSiteId') expected by the EcomAuthenticatedHeaders type and core services.
bugs.risk: Core services and client factories expect the camel-case properties produced by the standard schema parser. Providing kebab-case keys will result in 'undefined' values when the service attempts to access 'headers.baseSiteId', causing failed API requests.

bugs.title: Inconsistent Key Access on queryParamsData
bugs.description: The Salesforce path in 'get-orders' accesses 'user-id' (kebab-case) and 'orderId' (camel-case) from the same 'queryParamsData' object. This is highly inconsistent and suggests a mapping error.
bugs.risk: One of these lookups is likely to return 'undefined'. If the schema does not transform 'user-id' to 'userId', then 'orderId' should likely be 'order-id' (or vice versa), leading to missing order IDs or user IDs in the resulting service call.

notBugs.reason: The naming 'BodySafesForceSchema' is likely a typo for 'Salesforce', but it is used consistently across imports and usage, so it is not a functional bug.

Using .includes('/v1/orders/cancel-sf') might catch multiple Salesforce routes (like partial-cancel), but if the intent is to apply the same Salesforce-specific logic to all such routes, it is not a bug.
